In 43 patients with epilepsy, electrical stimulation evoked painful sensations from the upper posterior insula in 14 patients, mostly in the right hemisphere, and non-painful somatic sensations from the posterior insula in 16, so painful and non-painful representations overlap, with a trend toward somatotopy (human).

Bilateral anterior insula, rostral anterior cingulate cortex, brainstem and cerebellum responded both when subjects received pain and when a signal showed that their loved one was receiving it, and anterior insula and cingulate responses correlated with empathy scores, whereas posterior insula/secondary somatosensory, sensorimotor and caudal cingulate cortex responded only to one's own pain (human).

Meta-analyses of fMRI studies of empathy for pain (9 image-based, 32 coordinate-based) found a core network of bilateral anterior insula and medial/anterior cingulate cortex whose activation overlaps with that during directly experienced pain (human).

Inhaling odorants that produce a strong feeling of disgust and watching video clips of others' facial expressions of disgust activated the same sites in the anterior insula, and to a lesser extent in the anterior cingulate cortex (human).
A patient with damage to the insula and putamen provided evidence for a neural system that recognizes social signals of disgust from multiple modalities (human).

Task-free connectivity analyses identified a salience network anchored by dorsal anterior cingulate and orbital frontoinsular cortices, with robust connectivity to subcortical and limbic structures, and a separate executive-control network; prescan anxiety correlated with connectivity of the dorsal anterior cingulate node of the salience network (human).

In auditory, visual oddball and resting-state fMRI, a network of right fronto-insular and anterior cingulate cortex was activated by salient events, and chronometry and Granger causality analysis indicated that the right fronto-insular cortex plays a critical and causal role in switching between the central-executive and default-mode networks (human).

Review: proposes that the anterior insula is the hub of a salience network with the anterior cingulate cortex that detects salient events, switches between large-scale networks to give access to attention and working memory, modulates autonomic reactivity through interaction of the anterior and posterior insula, and gives rapid access to the motor system.

Frontotemporal dementia, which injures anterior cingulate and frontoinsular cortex early, the only homes of the von Economo neurons found in great apes and humans, caused early, severe and selective loss of anterior cingulate von Economo neurons (74% fewer per section than in controls), whereas Alzheimer's disease did not (human).

Hypothesis: individuals prone to anxiety show an augmented interoceptive prediction signal, the difference between observed and expected body state, which triggers anxious affect, worry and avoidance; the anterior insula is proposed to play a key role in this process.

Insular cortex neurons of behaving mice responded preferentially to food cues when hungry but not when sated; activating hypothalamic AgRP hunger neurons restored hunger-like responses, through a pathway via the paraventricular thalamus and basolateral amygdala (mouse).

During hunger and thirst, ongoing activity of mouse insular cortex tracked the gradual return to homeostasis rather than changes in behaviour, and food or water cues shifted it toward the future satiety-related pattern, suggesting that insular cortex combines visceral signals of the current state with hypothalamus-gated amygdala inputs to predict the future physiological state (mouse).

The mouse posterior insula processed aversive sensory stimuli and emotional and bodily states and exerted top-down modulation of ongoing behaviour; its projection to the central amygdala mediated anxiety-related behaviours, and an independent nucleus accumbens-projecting pathway regulated feeding upon changes in bodily state (mouse).

The rhesus insula has agranular, dysgranular and granular architectonic sectors, the granular one covering its posterior part, arranged with lateral orbital and temporopolar cortex around prepiriform allocortex as a paralimbic belt; the authors note that the human insula has a virtually identical plan (monkey).

The rhesus insula receives cortical input from prefrontal, lateral orbital, frontoparietal opercular, cingulate, prepiriform olfactory, temporopolar, superior temporal sulcus, rhinal, supratemporal and posterior parietal cortex (monkey).

The rhesus insula sends efferents back to the areas that project to it, linking it with olfactory, gustatory, somatosensory and auditory areas, visual, auditory and somatosensory association cortex, premotor cortex and paralimbic areas; its posterodorsal part relates to auditory, somesthetic and skeletomotor function and its anteroventral part to olfactory, gustatory and autonomic function, and through its connections with the amygdala it gives somatosensory, auditory, gustatory, olfactory and visceral sensations a route to the limbic system (monkey).

Review: in primates the insula connects with orbital, opercular, premotor, somatosensory, temporal and cingulate cortex and with the lateral, basolateral, central, cortical and medial amygdaloid nuclei; the thalamic taste area (the parvicellular ventral posteromedial nucleus) projects to insular-opercular cortex, and the insula has been confirmed as a visceral sensory, visceral motor, motor association, vestibular and language area with an expanded somatosensory role.

Meta-analysis of 1,768 neuroimaging experiments found four functionally distinct insular regions, sensorimotor (mid-posterior), social-emotional (anterior-ventral), olfacto-gustatory (central) and cognitive (anterior-dorsal), and all functions except basic somatosensory and motor processes overlapped on the anterior-dorsal insula (human).

When subjects were led to expect a highly aversive bitter taste to be less distasteful, they rated it less aversive and the primary taste cortex (insula and operculum) responded less, and right insula/operculum activity tracked aversiveness ratings (human).

Meta-analysis of 193 voxel-based morphometry studies (15,892 people, six diagnostic groups) found gray matter loss converging across diagnoses in the dorsal anterior cingulate and both insulae, a network tightly interconnected in healthy people, in whom lower gray matter there was associated with poorer executive function (human).

Multisensory integration in mouse insular cortex was robust in C57BL/6 mice but impaired in the BTBR model of idiopathic autism, reflecting weakened GABA circuits and incomplete postnatal pruning of cross-modal input; transient diazepam in an early sensitive period rescued it, and GAD65, Shank3 and Mecp2 knockout mice were also impaired (mouse).

On the Cambridge Gamble Task, patients with insular cortex lesions failed to adjust their bets to the odds of winning and went bankrupt more often, whereas patients with ventromedial prefrontal lesions bet more regardless of the odds (human).

Resting-state connectivity divided the insula into a ventral-anterior network, linked to middle and inferior temporal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex and limbic regions, and a middle-posterior network, linked to premotor, sensorimotor, supplementary motor and mid-posterior cingulate cortex (human).

Cloning identified 18 members of an extremely large multigene family encoding seven-transmembrane-domain proteins whose expression is restricted to the olfactory epithelium and which are likely to encode a diverse family of odorant receptors (rat).

Genetically labelled axons of sensory neurons expressing a given odorant receptor projected to only two topographically fixed loci among about 1800 glomeruli in the mouse olfactory bulb, and receptor-swap experiments suggest that the receptor plays an instructive role in guiding them but is not the sole determinant of the map (mouse).

Information from about 1000 odorant receptor types, organized in the nose into four zones of randomly scattered neurons, is transformed in the olfactory bulb into a highly organized spatial map: specific receptor probes label small, distinct subsets of glomeruli, and the authors propose an epitope map whose components are used in combinations to discriminate odours (mouse).

Axons from sensory neurons expressing a given odorant receptor converge on one, or at most a few, glomeruli whose positions are bilaterally symmetric and constant across individuals, supporting a model in which each odorant is associated with a specific topographic pattern of glomerular activity (rat).

One odorant receptor recognized multiple odorants and one odorant was recognized by multiple receptors, but different odorants were recognized by different combinations of receptors, so odour identities are encoded combinatorially; slight changes in an odorant or its concentration can change its code (mouse).

Tracing from individual glomeruli showed that their axons project diffusely across the piriform cortex without apparent spatial preference, whereas projections to the cortical amygdala form broad, spatially stereotyped and overlapping patches (mouse).

Trans-synaptic tracing showed that individual olfactory cortex neurons receive input from multiple mitral cells representing broadly distributed glomeruli; the cortical amygdala preferentially receives dorsal bulb input, whereas the piriform cortex samples the whole bulb without obvious bias (mouse).

Activating a small, arbitrarily chosen subpopulation of piriform neurons, paired with reward or shock, came to elicit appetitive or aversive behaviour, and different subpopulations could be trained to elicit distinct behaviours, so the piriform cortex is sufficient to elicit learned behaviour without sensory input and does not appear to use spatial order to map odour identity (mouse).

A stereotyped circuit from the olfactory bulb to the cortical amygdala was necessary for innate aversive and appetitive responses to odours, and optically activating cortical amygdala neurons that innate odours had activated recapitulated those behaviours (mouse).

Mice whose dorsal-zone sensory neurons were ablated, leaving the dorsal olfactory bulb without glomeruli, lacked innate responses to aversive odorants although they detected them and could be conditioned to avoid them, so separate glomeruli serve innate and learned aversive responses (mouse).

Distributed ensemble activity in human posterior piriform cortex matched perceptual ratings of odour quality, so that odorants with more similar fMRI patterns were perceived as more alike, an effect not seen in anterior piriform cortex, amygdala or orbitofrontal cortex (human).

Sniffing, with or without an odorant, activated mainly the piriform cortex and the medial and posterior orbitofrontal gyri, driven by the somatosensory stimulation of airflow through the nostrils, whereas a smell, regardless of sniffing, activated mainly the lateral and anterior orbitofrontal gyri (human).

Odorants activated the cerebellum, mainly the posterior lateral hemispheres and more for higher concentrations, whereas sniffing odourless air activated the anterior cerebellum, mainly the central lobule; the authors propose that the cerebellum regulates sniff volume according to odour concentration (human).

Olfactory stimulation increased blood flow bilaterally at the junction of the inferior frontal and temporal lobes, corresponding to the piriform cortex, and in the right orbitofrontal cortex, indicating a right-sided asymmetry of orbitofrontal olfactory processing (human).

In 1955 people aged 5 to 99, smell identification peaked in the third to fifth decades and declined markedly after the seventh; more than half of those aged 65 to 80 and more than three-quarters of those over 80 had major olfactory impairment, and women outperformed men and nonsmokers outperformed smokers (human).

Meta-analysis of 43 studies found severe deficits in odour identification, recognition and detection threshold in both Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, with no difference between the diseases or among the three domains (human).

In 2,267 men aged 71 to 95 followed for up to 8 years, poor odour identification predicted Parkinson's disease within the first 4 years (odds ratio 5.2 for the lowest versus the top two quartiles) but not later, so impaired smell can precede clinical Parkinson's disease by at least 4 years (human).
Subventricular zone cells from the lateral ventricle of adult mice, grafted or labelled in place, migrated long distances and differentiated into neurons in the olfactory bulb (mouse).

Continuous adult neurogenesis replaced the majority of olfactory bulb granule neurons and added granule neurons to the dentate gyrus; ablating new neurons gradually reduced bulb granule cells, prevented the growth of the dentate gyrus and impaired contextual and spatial memory (mouse).

In rat olfactory bulb slices, glutamate released from mitral cell dendrites excites granule cell dendrites, which return GABAergic dendrodendritic inhibition; this inhibition depends critically on NMDA receptors and on N- and P/Q-type calcium channels, scales with dendritic calcium influx, and can mediate lateral inhibition between mitral cells without axonal action potentials (rat).
Rats discriminating odours reached maximal accuracy within a single sniff (under 200 ms), and the speed of discrimination did not depend on odour similarity, even with difficult mixtures (rat).

Olfactory mucosa of mice, non-human primates and humans expressed the SARS-CoV-2 entry genes ACE2 and TMPRSS2, but single-cell sequencing placed ACE2 in support, stem and perivascular cells rather than in neurons, suggesting that COVID-19 anosmia results from infection of non-neuronal cells (mouse, monkey, human).

Sensory activation of mouse vomeronasal neurons required the ion channel TRP2, and TRP2-deficient males showed no male-male aggression and initiated sexual and courtship behaviour toward both males and females, suggesting that vomeronasal activation is essential for sex discrimination (mouse).

Olfactory bulb stimulation evoked potentials in the lateroposterior orbitofrontal cortex that depended on the anterior piriform cortex (probably with the medial amygdala) and the hypothalamus but not the thalamus, and removing this orbitofrontal area strikingly impaired odour discrimination (monkey).

After a food was eaten to satiety, the activation of a region of orbitofrontal cortex by the odour of that food decreased, whereas the activation by the odour of a food not eaten did not, linking orbitofrontal activation to olfactory sensory-specific satiety (human).

Intracranial recordings in epilepsy patients showed that natural nasal breathing synchronizes oscillations in piriform cortex, amygdala and hippocampus, with power peaking during inspiration and fading when breathing was diverted to the mouth; in behavioural experiments, breathing phase enhanced fear discrimination and memory retrieval (human).

As rats learned to use an odour cue to guide navigation, 20 to 40 Hz coherence developed between the lateral entorhinal cortex and distal CA1, the subfields that receive the predominant olfactory input to the hippocampal region, together with ensemble representations of trial outcomes in each (rat).

Review: the identification, categorization and discrimination of odours appear to rely on the formation and modulation of odour objects in the piriform cortex, and human and rodent findings suggest that distributed piriform ensemble patterns maintain perceptual constancy.

Four years after baseline, 7% of people with idiopathic smell loss had developed Parkinson's disease and 13% showed motor abnormalities, suggesting that olfactory testing combined with other tests may screen for the risk of the disease (human).

In rat piriform cortex, odours evoked sparse spiking because inhibition was widespread and broadly tuned while excitation was less common and odour-specific; respiration imposed a slow rhythm on responses, and odours evoked fast (15 to 30 Hz) oscillations in which excitation preceded inhibition (rat).

Review: olfactory dysfunction is among the earliest nonmotor features of Parkinson's disease, present in about 90% of early-stage cases and preceding motor symptoms by years; equivalent deficits occur in Alzheimer's disease, and smell loss correlates with fewer neurons in the locus coeruleus, raphe nuclei and nucleus basalis.

Phasic optogenetic activation of the locus coeruleus strengthened correlations between gustatory cortex responses and palatability and expanded the range of taste representations along a palatability axis, through an aversive shift of every tastant except sucrose, whereas tonic activation affected fewer neurons and did not expand the attribute axes (mouse).

In water-restricted mice licking novel or familiar tastants, noradrenergic locus coeruleus activity was suppressed during lick bursts and transiently rose when licking stopped, regardless of novelty, and brief unexpected tastants did not activate it although visual and auditory stimuli did; the authors suggest a possible role for noradrenergic nuclei other than the locus coeruleus in signalling critical information about taste (mouse).

A histological atlas of the adult Octopus minor brain, from serial sagittal and coronal sections stained with haematoxylin and eosin, delineated more than 70 subregions; the authors describe it as the first brain atlas for any adult cephalopod (octopus).

High angular resolution diffusion MRI tractography of three Octopus bimaculoides brains, segmented into 25 lobes, found 92 connections between lobes (53 among supra-oesophageal lobes and 26 between the optic lobes and other structures), largely agreeing with earlier studies, except that connections between the vertical lobe and more basal supra-oesophageal structures were not found (octopus).

A phylogenetically informed imaging comparison of diurnal and nocturnal coastal and deep-sea octopus species linked enlargement and division of the optic lobe and structural folding of the central brain to behaviour and habitat, with phylogeny possibly playing a part; the difference between solitary and social life was mirrored in the brain, including multiple compartments (gyri) in the vertical lobe, which the authors liken to the vertebrate cortex (octopus).

Horseradish peroxidase tracing showed that the optic lobe receives input from the anterior, median and dorsal basal, interbasal, subvertical, precommissural, brachial and magnocellular lobes, the contralateral optic lobe, optic tract lobes and photoreceptors of the ipsilateral retina, and sends fibres to the superior frontal and lateral basal lobes; fibres partly from the posterior subvertical lobe were labelled in the neuropil of vertical lobules (octopus).

Review: summarizes molecular, anatomical and developmental data and, from body and brain axes defined in early embryos, describes cephalopod neural systems that show similarities to the vertebrate cerebral cortex, thalamus, basal ganglia, midbrain, cerebellum, hypothalamus, brain stem and spinal cord, while how far a vertebrate equivalence exists remains unanswered.

In Octopus bimaculoides the peduncle complex rests on the optic tract between the optic lobe and the central brain and comprises the peduncle lobe, which regulates visuomotor behaviour, the olfactory lobe, thought to receive input from the olfactory organ, and the optic gland, which controls sexual maturation and maternal death; optic gland peptide and steroid pathways extended beyond the gland into lobular territories, and the olfactory lobe included steroidogenic territories overlapping cells expressing molluscan neuropeptides and dopamine beta-hydroxylase (octopus).

A cell type atlas of the paralarval Octopus vulgaris brain mapped neural cells, several glial subtypes, endothelial cells and fibroblasts to the vertical, subesophageal and optic lobes; vertical lobe cells were enriched for learning- and memory-related genes and showed molecular similarities with Drosophila Kenyon cells, and glia shared a gene signature with mouse and fly glia (octopus).

Single-cell RNA sequencing with RNA in situ hybridization of the Octopus bimaculoides optic lobe, the primary visual processing structure, revealed six major neuronal classes defined by neurotransmitter or neuropeptide use, subtypes with distinct laminar locations, and immature neurons in this continuously growing tissue (octopus).

The Octopus bimaculoides genome showed no whole-genome duplications but massive expansions of the protocadherins, which regulate neuronal development, and of C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factors, extensive mRNA editing in genes for neural excitability and other functions, and hundreds of cephalopod-specific genes, many highly expressed in skin, suckers and the nervous system (octopus).

In brain slices of the vertical lobe, an area involved in learning and memory, field potential recordings revealed long-term potentiation of glutamatergic synaptic field potentials similar to that in vertebrates (octopus).

methods: tetanization of the vertical lobe pathway
finding: Tetanizing the vertical lobe pathway to enhance its synapses globally accelerated short-term learning of a passive avoidance task, whereas transecting the pathway slowed it, but both impaired long-term recall the next day, suggesting that the vertical lobe acquires long-term memory through LTP and also modulates short-term learning (Octopus vulgaris).

In both Octopus vulgaris and the cuttlefish Sepia officinalis the vertical lobe has the same fan-out fan-in architecture of three neuron types, but synaptic plasticity lies at the fan-out glutamatergic layer in the octopus and at the fan-in cholinergic layer in the cuttlefish; the linear input-output relations of the intermediate-layer neurons let both networks perform the same computation (octopus, cuttlefish).

Serotonin-immunoreactive afferent terminals innervate the neuropil, but not the cell bodies, of the vertical lobe, and 5-HT (effective at a high, 100 µM concentration) facilitated synaptic transmission and activity-dependent LTP induction without clear long-term facilitation; the authors propose it is part of a reinforcing or reward signalling system (Octopus vulgaris).

Review: JZ Young described the morphological convergence of the cephalopod vertical lobe with the mammalian hippocampus, the cerebellum and the insect mushroom body; octopus and cuttlefish vertical lobes share a fan-out fan-in network with activity-dependent long-term plasticity, but their neurons, transmitters, neuromodulators and LTP mechanisms vary between species.

Histolabeling of the vertical lobe confirmed glutamatergic median superior frontal lobe inputs and cholinergic amacrine interneurons, with intense nitric oxide synthase activity in amacrine neurites in line with NO-dependent presynaptic LTP; it also found GABAergic amacrines, GABA in large output neurons that co-express FMRFamide-like peptides, a glutamatergic group of output neurons and a catecholaminergic "deep nucleus" (Octopus vulgaris).

Serial-section electron microscopy of a small volume of the Octopus vulgaris vertical lobe found that about 1.8 million input axons sparsely innervate two interconnected feedforward networks: simple amacrine cells (89.3% of the lobe's roughly 25 million cells), each receiving input from a single input axon at a likely LTP "memory site", and newly described complex amacrine cells (1.6%) that integrate many inputs and appear to provide balancing inhibition to the output layer (octopus).

Untrained octopuses that watched trained conspecifics choose between two objects differing only in colour then chose the same object, irrespective of which colour the demonstrators had been trained on and faster than by conditioning, showing observational learning in an invertebrate (Octopus vulgaris).

Removing about 50% of the vertical lobe impaired performance after observational learning of a visual discrimination, but performance improved 24 h later; the authors conclude that the lesion impairs short-term recall but not acquisition or retention of observational long-term memory (Octopus vulgaris).

The muscarinic antagonist scopolamine did not affect predation on live crabs but impaired memory recall: solving the jar problem within the first hour after injection (partly recovered after 24 h) and both individually and observationally learned visual discriminations (Octopus vulgaris).

Intramuscular injection of a nitric oxide synthase inhibitor completely blocked touch learning: eight control animals learned a touch paradigm and none of eight inhibitor-treated animals did, the first evidence that nitric oxide is essential for learning in an invertebrate (Octopus vulgaris).

methods: implanted electrodes with a data logger in freely moving animals
finding: A data logger inserted into the octopus recorded activity from electrodes in the vertical lobe system for up to 12 h in unanaesthetized, untethered animals, synchronized with video; distinct activity patterns appeared consistently, some resembling mammalian patterns and others, such as episodes of 2 Hz large-amplitude oscillations, not reported before (octopus).

Two-photon calcium imaging of the optic lobe, the primary visual processing centre, found spatially localized receptive fields for light (ON) and dark (OFF) stimuli, retinotopically organized, with the OFF pathway and greater size selectivity emerging across the layers of the optic lobe and asymmetries in spatial processing of ON and OFF stimuli (octopus).
Per its title (PubMed lists no abstract): the peduncle lobe is a visuo-motor centre in the octopus (octopus).

Arm extensions evoked mechanically or electrically in arms whose connection with the brain had been severed showed kinematic features almost identical to normal behaviour, suggesting that the basic motor program for voluntary arm extension is embedded in the neural circuitry of the arm itself (octopus).

When fetching food to the mouth, octopus arms form a quasi-articulated structure with three dynamic joints; two waves of muscle activation propagate toward each other and their collision point sets the medial joint, and kinematic invariants appear at the joint level, as in certain human arm movements (octopus).

methods: brain microstimulation in freely behaving animals
finding: Microstimulation of the basal lobes, the higher motor centres, in freely behaving octopuses evoked discrete and complex movements, recruited from shared basic components as stimulation strength increased, but no site evoked movement of a single arm or body part, so these centres show no central topographical organization (octopus).

In a three-choice maze that required a single arm to reach a visually marked goal compartment, octopuses guided one arm through a complex movement to the goal, showing that they combine peripheral arm location information with visual input to control goal-directed movement (Octopus vulgaris).

In two-choice single-arm mazes that mimic tactile exploration, the central nervous system used peripheral information about arm motion as well as tactile input to learn tasks requiring directed arm movement; only about one third of octopus neurons are central, the rest lying in the peripheral nervous system including the eight arms, yet the arms are subject to central control (Octopus vulgaris).

Kinematic analysis of crawling showed that octopuses can crawl in any direction relative to their body orientation, control body and crawling orientation independently, and coordinate their arms without apparent rhythmic patterns, the central controller choosing moment to moment which arms push the body by elongation (octopus).

The oral intramuscular nerve cords of each arm, thought to include proprioceptive neurons and motoneurons, continue beyond the arm base, bypass the two adjacent arms and join the nearer oral cord of the third arm over, so each arm connects to the arms two away on either side; the aboral cords also extend beyond the arm base (octopus).

The axial nerve cord of the octopus arm is segmented: its neurons form segments along the cord, nerves exit in the septa between segments, and for each sucker they form a spatial topographic map ('suckerotopy'); comparison with squid arms and tentacles links segmentation to flexible sucker-laden arms (octopus, squid).

The sucker ganglion in the stalk of every sucker contains cell bodies expressing sensory (PIEZO) and motor (LHX3, MNX) neuron markers, and its nerve fibres target the sucker musculature and the oral roots extending to the axial nerve cord; the authors suggest it facilitates local reflexes for each sucker rather than being a simple relay (Octopus bimaculoides).

Suckers of amputated arms never attached to octopus skin because a chemical in the skin inhibits the sucker attachment reflex; behaving octopuses sometimes overrode this and grabbed amputated arms, and treated arms of other octopuses like food more often than their own (octopus).

Review: argues that the octopus's long, flexible arms, with their infinite degrees of freedom, have imposed unique brain-body-behaviour relationships best explained as intelligent behaviour emerging from the animal's embodied organization.

Review: almost 30 years of research on Octopus vulgaris motor control show that the higher motor control centres coordinate limbs with large numbers of degrees of freedom without using body-part maps to represent sensory and motor information, as vertebrates do, through control embodied in the body morphology.

methods: isolated nerve tract stimulation and recording
finding: In isolated cerebrobrachial tracts connecting the brain and the arms, electrical activity and contraction of a small attached muscle strand were evoked at low threshold regardless of stimulus direction and distance, suggesting that axons carrying motor commands run along the tract and innervate a large pool of motor neurons en passant (Octopus vulgaris).

Octopus arms use a family of cephalopod-specific chemotactile receptors, which form discrete ion channel complexes, to detect poorly soluble natural products on contact ('taste by touch'), and distinct chemo- and mechanosensory cells with specific receptor expression and electrical activity support peripheral information coding (octopus).

A cryo-electron microscopy structure of an octopus chemotactile receptor, which diverged from nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, showed a conserved channel architecture but a ligand-binding site under diversifying selection, with an exceptionally hydrophobic binding pocket suited to sensing greasy compounds (octopus).

Octopus 'quiet' sleep is interrupted by bouts of about 60 s of 'active' sleep that are homeostatically regulated, rapidly reversible and have a raised arousal threshold, with skin patterns strongly resembling waking ones; local field potentials during active sleep resemble waking, strongest in the superior frontal and vertical lobes, which in quiet sleep are relatively silent but generate oscillations resembling mammalian sleep spindles (octopus).

In Octopus insularis a 'quiet sleep' state with pale skin, closed pupils and long episodes alternated with short 'active sleep' episodes (median 40.8 s) with dynamic skin colour and texture and rapid eye movements; active sleep recurred periodically (60% of recurrences 26 to 39 min apart) and mostly followed quiet sleep, suggesting an ultradian sleep cycle analogous to that of amniotes (octopus).

Maternal behaviours of brooding female octopuses are eradicated if the optic glands, the octopus analogue of the pituitary, are removed; across behavioural stages the optic gland up- and downregulated catecholamine, steroid, insulin and feeding peptide pathways, changes that were not general markers of senescence in other tissues (Octopus bimaculoides).

The optic glands control lifespan and reproduction, and their removal reverses the post-mating course of brooding, fasting, self-injury and death; after reproduction, female optic glands mobilized at least three steroidogenic pathways, producing pregnane steroids, 7-dehydrocholesterol and bile acid intermediates (Octopus bimaculoides).

MDMA enhanced acute prosocial behaviour in Octopus bimaculoides, a member of a predominantly asocial and solitary order, paralleled by evolutionary conservation of the MDMA binding site of the serotonin transporter in its genome, suggesting that serotonergic transmission has a conserved role in social behaviour (octopus).

Octopuses avoided a context in which pain was experienced, preferred one where they experienced relief and showed no conditioned preference without pain, and grooming of an acetic acid injection site was abolished by local anaesthesia, suggesting that octopuses experience the affective component of pain (octopus).

After arm injury the octopus Abdopus aculeatus showed nocifensive behaviours including arm autotomy and neural hyperexcitability in both injured and uninjured arms for at least 24 h; the authors note that this does not demonstrate pain-like states (octopus).

In Octopus vulgaris embryos an important pool of neural progenitors expressing achaete-scute or neurogenin lies outside the central brain cords, in the lateral lips next to the eyes, and lineage tracing showed that, depending on their location in the lips, progenitors generate neurons for the different lobes, as in the squid Doryteuthis pealeii, and that newborn neurons migrate over long distances, reminiscent of vertebrate neurogenesis (octopus).

A neuronal wiring diagram of a whole adult female Drosophila brain, reconstructed from electron microscopy, contains 139,255 neurons and 5 × 10^7 chemical synapses annotated with cell classes and types, nerves, hemilineages and predicted neurotransmitters; tracing from sensory inputs to motor, endocrine and descending outputs, and from photoreceptors to descending motor pathways, illustrates how structure can suggest circuit mechanisms (fly).

A connectome of a large fraction of the adult fly brain gives detailed circuits of neurons and their chemical synapses for most of the central brain, defines cell types and computational compartments with an atlas of examples, and analyses connection-strength distributions and motifs on several scales (fly).

methods: network analysis of the whole-brain connectome
finding: Network analysis of the whole-brain connectome of an adult fly found rich-club organization, with a large population (30% of the connectome) of highly connected neurons, identified subsets of rich-club neurons that may act as integrators or broadcasters of signals, and examined subnetworks of 78 anatomically defined neuropils (fly).

methods: leaky integrate-and-fire model of the whole brain
finding: A leaky integrate-and-fire model of the entire fly brain, built only from synapse-level connectivity and predicted neurotransmitter identity, predicted the neurons that respond to sugar or water taste and are required for feeding initiation, and predicted neurons whose activation elicits motor neuron firing, a hypothesis validated by optogenetic activation and behaviour (fly).

Relating published connectome data to published whole-brain in vivo imaging of the central brain found a strong relationship between resting-state functional correlations and direct region-to-region structural connectivity; the correspondence varied across the brain, and some regions, including the mushroom body, depended more strongly on indirect connections (fly).

Calcium signals of spontaneous ("resting-state") activity recorded across the adult fly central brain, aligned to an anatomical atlas and correlated between regions, revealed an intrinsic functional network, a large-scale architecture for neural communication (fly).

SCAPE imaging of all cells in a large volume of the adult fly brain during spontaneous behaviour found that the activity of most neurons correlated or anticorrelated with running and flailing over seconds to a minute, while residual activity not directly tied to behaviour was high dimensional and came from small clusters of spatially organized neurons that also take part in the global dynamics (fly).

methods: electron microscopy connectome of the whole CNS
finding: The connectome of an entire male Drosophila central nervous system, brain and nerve cord, contains 166,700 proofread and annotated neurons of 11,710 types; compared with the female brain it found 8,069 isomorphic, 138 dimorphic, 289 male-specific and 71 female-specific types, with sex-specific and dimorphic neurons concentrated in higher brain centres and the sensory and motor periphery largely isomorphic (fly).

A complete wiring diagram of the male fly gustatory system, reconstructing gustatory receptor neurons from peripheral organs in an electron microscopy volume spanning brain, cervical connective and ventral nerve cord, mapped all feeding motor neurons and traced complete sensory-to-motor pathways to feeding, foraging, endocrine and social behaviour circuits (fly).

Drosophila odorant receptors are encoded by 57 genes; individual sensory neurons are likely to express a single receptor gene, and neurons expressing a given gene project axons to one or two spatially invariant glomeruli in the antennal lobe, so the brain retains a two-dimensional map of receptor activation (fly).

Or83b, a broadly expressed and conserved odorant receptor present with conventional receptors in most olfactory neurons, is needed for the dendritic localization of the conventional receptors, and its mutation disrupts behavioural and electrophysiological responses to many odorants (fly).

In vivo whole-cell recordings found that monomolecular odours elicit responses in large ensembles of antennal lobe neurons, and second-order neurons are more broadly tuned and respond more complexly than their afferents in the same glomerulus, implicating lateral interactions within the antennal lobe (fly).

methods: anatomical tracing of single Kenyon cell inputs
finding: Tracing the glomerular origin of the inputs to 200 individual Kenyon cells showed that each integrates input from a different, apparently random combination of olfactory glomeruli, with no discernible organization by odour tuning, anatomy or developmental origin (fly).

High-resolution maps of 35 projection-neuron input channels showed that PNs relay olfactory information to the mushroom body and lateral horn with stereotyped inputs to both; in the lateral horn fruit odours are represented mostly posterior-dorsally while candidate pheromone-responsive PNs project anterior-ventrally, suggesting it is organized by the biological value of olfactory input (fly).

Split-GAL4 lines for 82 lateral horn cell types, mapped anatomically and linked to EM connectomics, showed that about 30% of lateral horn projections converge with mushroom body outputs, and optogenetic activation identified LH cell types that drive changes in valence behaviour or specific locomotor programs (fly).

methods: tetanus toxin expression in projection neurons
finding: Expressing tetanus toxin in most projection neurons (and a few mushroom body neurons) caused defects in odour detection and male courtship; with data from flies lacking mushroom bodies, this argues that the direct pathway from PNs to the lateral protocerebrum is necessary and sufficient for these experience-independent behaviours (fly).

The male pheromone cVA acts through the receptor Or67d: mutant males lacking Or67d court other males and mutant females are less receptive, and replacing Or67d with moth pheromone receptors made these neurons respond to moth pheromones with cVA-like behaviour, so a single olfactory receptor neuron class is necessary and sufficient for behavioural responses to cVA (fly).

methods: hydroxyurea ablation of the mushroom bodies
finding: Ablating the mushroom bodies with hydroxyurea fed to newly hatched larvae left adult flies normal in most respects but unable to learn odour–shock associations in classical conditioning, a deficit not explained by reduced olfactory sensitivity, shock reactivity or locomotion (fly).

methods: temperature-sensitive shibire block of synaptic output
finding: Transiently blocking synaptic output of mushroom body α/β neurons with temperature-sensitive shibire showed that their signalling is required during olfactory memory retrieval, but not during acquisition or consolidation (fly).

methods: rutabaga mutants with Kenyon cell-restricted expression
finding: The rutabaga adenylyl cyclase, which mediates synaptic plasticity, is needed only in the Kenyon cells of the mushroom bodies for a component of olfactory short-term memory, showing that synaptic plasticity in a small brain region can be sufficient for memory formation (fly).

methods: genetic manipulation of cAMP signalling, dopamine and octopamine
finding: For both appetitive and aversive olfactory memories, cAMP signalling is necessary and sufficient in the same subpopulation of mushroom body intrinsic neurons, but aversive conditioning requires dopamine and appetitive conditioning requires octopamine (fly).

Dopamine neurons of the PAM cluster signal sugar reward: they are selectively required for the reinforcing property of sugar but not a reflexive response to it, are activated by sugar ingestion (more so on starvation), and have output sites mainly in the medial lobes of the mushroom bodies; the authors propose that they give odours a positive predictive value there (fly).

Octopamine reinforces only short-term appetitive memory and does so through dopamine neurons: part of its signal requires the OAMB receptor in a subset of mushroom-body-targeted dopamine neurons, whose direct activation can substitute for sugar to form appetitive memory even in flies lacking octopamine (fly).

A comprehensive map of the mushroom body: 21 output neuron (MBON) types arborize along the parallel axons of about 2,000 Kenyon cells in 15 compartments that tile the lobes, MBON axons project to five neuropils outside the MB, and each of 20 dopaminergic neuron types projects to one or at most two compartments, a unit that can support learning to impose valence on sensory representations (fly).

Optogenetic activation of mushroom body output neurons induced repulsion or attraction depending on cell type, and the behavioural effects of perturbing them in associative learning tasks were combinatorial; the authors suggest that the MBON ensemble collectively represents valence and biases memory-based action selection (fly).

methods: optogenetic pairing of odour and dopamine neuron activation
finding: Pairing an odour with activation of specific dopamine neurons induced learning and odour-specific synaptic depression at the mushroom body output site, the first demonstration there of long-term synaptic plasticity; induction depended on the temporal order of the two stimuli, and dopamine action was confined to, and differed between, the compartments of the MB lobes (fly).

methods: anatomical and functional screen of output neurons
finding: MB-V2 neurons, cholinergic output neurons projecting from the mushroom body vertical lobes to the middle superior medial protocerebrum and the lateral horn, were essential for retrieval of short- and long-lasting aversive odour memory but not for its formation or consolidation, and their odour responses changed after conditioning (fly).

In alpha-lobes-absent mutants, which lack either the two vertical lobes of the mushroom body or two of its median lobes, long-term memory required the vertical lobes but not the median lobes, and short-term memory was normal without either (fly).

methods: electron microscopy connectome of the mushroom body
finding: Analysis of the dense mushroom body connectome identified new components, including extensive visual input and output neurons with direct connections to descending neurons, structure in the transfer of sensory information to MBONs and in its modulation by dopaminergic neurons, connections between the MB and the central complex, and inputs to DANs including feedback from MBONs (fly).

methods: activation and blockade of Kenyon cells and APL
finding: Kenyon cells and the GABAergic APL neuron form a negative feedback loop, Kenyon cells activating APL and APL inhibiting them; disrupting it made Kenyon cell odour responses less sparse and more correlated and stopped flies learning to discriminate similar, but not dissimilar, odours (fly).

methods: two-photon calcium imaging in walking flies
finding: Imaging in flies walking in virtual reality showed that a population of neurons whose dendrites tile the ellipsoid body encodes the fly’s azimuth, tracking visual landmarks when available and self-motion in darkness, and keeps it by persistent activity when both cues are absent; its dynamics and circular layout suggest a ring attractor (fly).

methods: two-photon calcium imaging in walking and flying flies
finding: Central complex ring neurons have visually responsive, retinotopically arranged dendrites with excitatory and inhibitory subfields resembling those of simple cells in mammalian primary visual cortex, and strong, sometimes direction-selective orientation tuning that prefers vertical features; their responses were diminished in flight but not modulated by walking (fly).

methods: two-photon calcium imaging in flying flies
finding: Optogenetically overwriting the heading representation with an artificial bump of activity, which the circuit then maintained with naturalistic dynamics, showed that a network with local excitation and global inhibition enforces a unique and persistent heading representation: physiological evidence for a ring attractor (fly).

Clockwise- and anticlockwise-shifting neurons of the central complex, whose wiring and physiology can rotate the heading estimate according to angular velocity, are required for the heading system to track the fly’s heading in the dark, and stimulating them induces predictable shifts in the heading signal (fly).

Flies formed and retained visual place memories that guide navigation, and silencing small subsets of neurons showed that neurons in the ellipsoid body, but not in the mushroom bodies, are necessary for visual place learning (fly).

Short-term memory traces for two visual pattern parameters, elevation and contour orientation, were localized to two groups of neurons forming parallel horizontal strata in the fan-shaped body, which contains part of a network mediating visual pattern recognition (fly).

In a detour task, flies remembered the position of an object for several seconds after it was removed; the GABAergic ring neurons of the ellipsoid body were necessary, and their plasticity sufficient, for this spatial orientation memory, which also requires the kinase S6KII in a subset of ring neurons (fly).

methods: electron microscopy connectome of the central complex
finding: The first complete electron microscopy connectome of the fly central complex identified new neuron types, sensory and motor pathways, and network motifs likely to extract head direction, maintain it with attractor dynamics and combine it with other information for vector-based navigation, plus many pathways that may let context and internal state select CX-driven behaviour (fly).

The anterior visual pathway runs from visual projection neurons of the medulla to neurons of two lineages (DALcl1, DALcl2) that connect the anterior optic tubercle with the ring (R) neurons whose axons largely form the ellipsoid body; the two lineages form parallel channels with different receptive fields that may encode the position of a bright feature such as a celestial body (fly).

In a flight simulator flies held arbitrary headings relative to a simulated sun (menotaxis) and remembered their preference between flights; E-PG compass neurons tracked the sun stimulus, and silencing them abolished menotaxis, leaving frontal phototaxis (fly).

In the fan-shaped body, PFNd and PFNv neurons conjunctively encode translational velocity and heading by multiplying velocity signals from locomotor brain regions with compass heading signals; their convergence onto hΔB neurons rotates body-centric velocity into a world-centric representation, and perturbing PFNd neurons disrupts path integration in walking flies (fly).

Fly rest shares features of mammalian sleep: an increased arousal threshold, homeostatic regulation independent of the circadian clock, decline with age and modulation by stimulants and hypnotics, and flies lacking arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase show increased rest after rest deprivation (fly).

Thermogenetic activation of neurons, including those projecting to the dorsal fan-shaped body, induced sleep, and 4 hours of induced sleep after a massed courtship-conditioning protocol that cannot by itself produce long-term memory let flies form one; activating the dorsal FB without sleep did not (fly).

A subset of ellipsoid body neurons generates sleep drive when activated; sleep loss switches them from spiking to burst firing and reversibly raises their cytosolic Ca2+, NMDA receptor expression and structural markers of synaptic strength, and this plasticity is necessary and sufficient for generating sleep drive (fly).

Enhancing cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA) activity specifically in the adult mushroom bodies produced large changes in sleep, and electrically silencing, exciting or ablating the mushroom bodies also altered sleep (fly).

A screen blocking synaptic output in discrete neural circuits found three short-sleep lines whose shared expression was in the mushroom bodies, and chemical ablation of the mushroom bodies also reduced sleep (fly).

methods: electron microscopy connectome of the medulla
finding: An electron microscopy connectome of 379 neurons and 8,637 chemical synaptic contacts in the optic medulla, assembled into the repeating module of the medulla, identified the cell types of a motion detection circuit whose connections onto individual motion-sensitive neurons were consistent with their direction selectivity (fly).

methods: calcium imaging of T4 and T5
finding: Calcium imaging showed that subpopulations of T4 and T5 cells are each tuned to one of the four cardinal directions and terminate in matching lobula plate sublayers; T4 responds to moving ON edges and T5 to OFF edges, and blocking either selectively impaired downstream lobula plate responses and turning to ON or OFF motion (fly).

methods: genetic block and reconstitution of lamina neurons
finding: In the lamina, where photoreceptor signals split into five parallel pathways (L1–L5), blocking L1 output eliminated downstream responses to moving ON edges and blocking L2 output responses to moving OFF edges, so photoreceptor signals segregate into ON (L1) and OFF (L2) channels (fly).

Review: fly and mammalian motion vision share a circuit design, with motion extracted in parallel ON and OFF pathways, elementary motion detection by correlating signals with different temporal dynamics, and convergence onto four groups of ON–OFF neurons selective for the four cardinal directions (fly and mammals).

methods: optogenetic activation in freely moving flies
finding: 22 types of lobula columnar (LC) visual projection neurons project to distinct optic glomeruli; optogenetic activation of several types evoked specific behaviours, two resembling natural loom-avoidance, imaging showed that those two respond to looming while another type responds to small-object motion, and one-sided activation caused attractive or aversive turning depending on type (fly).

LPLC2 neurons detect looming with high selectivity through radial motion opponency: each arm of their cross-shaped dendrites ramifies in one of the four direction-selective T4/T5 layers of the lobula plate, outward motion excites them and inward motion inhibits them, and as a population they terminate onto the giant fibre descending neurons that drive escape take-off (fly).

methods: intracellular recording of the giant fibre during escape
finding: Faced with a looming stimulus, flies make either a long escape sequence that initiates stable flight or a short one that sacrifices stability for speed, and recordings from the descending giant fibre showed that its spike timing relative to parallel escape circuits determines which is chosen (fly).

methods: focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy connectome of the optic lobe
finding: A connectome of the right optic lobe of a male fly, acquired by focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy, classified about 53,000 visual neurons into 732 types, about half newly named, with an inventory of their anatomy and matched split-GAL4 lines (fly).

In the first relay of the fly brain, gustatory projections are segregated by taste category, with sugar-sensing neurons projecting to a different region from those recognizing noxious substances, and by the location of the taste neurons in the periphery (fly).

methods: in vivo calcium imaging of taste cells
finding: In vivo calcium imaging showed that Gr5a taste cells respond selectively to sugars and Gr66a cells to bitter compounds, and inducibly activating these neurons was sufficient to drive taste behaviours, so taste cells are tuned by category and hardwired to acceptance or avoidance (fly).

An unbiased activation screen identified a single pair of brain feeding (Fdg) neurons whose activation induces the entire feeding sequence and whose suppression or ablation eliminates sugar-induced feeding; they respond to food presentation only in starved flies, placing them downstream of sensory and metabolic cues and at the top of the feeding motor hierarchy (fly).

A silencing screen identified a pair of motor neurons in the subesophageal ganglion that control a subprogram of a simple taste behaviour; they are activated by sugar stimulation of gustatory neurons and inhibited by bitter compounds, but split-GFP detected no direct connections between them and the primary sensory neurons (fly).

methods: transgenic lines for individual descending neuron types
finding: Over 100 transgenic lines targeting individual descending neuron (DN) types, which link the brain to the body through the neck, identified roughly half of all fly DNs and mapped their connectivity between sensory neuropils in the brain and motor neuropils in the nerve cord, a layered system reflecting walking and flight (fly).

Descending MDN neurons are required for flies to walk backward at an impassable barrier and sufficient to trigger backward walking when flies would otherwise walk forward, and ascending MAN neurons promote persistent backward walking (fly).

fruitless alleles constitutively spliced in the male or female mode showed that male splicing is essential for male courtship behaviour and sexual orientation and sufficient to make otherwise normal females court other females (fly).

The male-specific FruM proteins, expressed in about 2% of central neurons and in subsets of all peripheral sensory systems implicated in courtship, specify its neural substrates: inactivating all FruM-expressing neurons abolishes courtship without other gross behavioural changes, and masculinizing them in females largely confers male courtship (fly).

First- and second-order olfactory neurons respond identically to the pheromone cVA in males and females, but two clusters of third-order olfactory neurons respond dimorphically, one in females and the other in males; by regulating dendrite position, fruitless connects the male-responsive cluster to pheromone input and disconnects the female-responsive one (fly).

Fly populations trained with two odours, one paired with electric shock, then avoided the shock-paired odour; non-associative explanations were ruled out, retraining extinguished the avoidance, the memory lasted 24 hours, and flies also learned to discriminate light sources of different colours (fly).
An X-linked mutant, dunce, fails to learn to avoid an odour paired with electric shock even though it can sense the odour and the shock and behaves essentially normally in other respects (fly).

methods: learning, cAMP metabolism and fertility mutants
finding: Independent searches for mutations of olfactory learning, of cyclic AMP metabolism and of female fertility each led to the same gene, dunce, which the evidence suggests encodes a cyclic AMP phosphodiesterase (fly).

rutabaga, an X-linked recessive mutation that blocks associative learning, affects adenylate cyclase: the mutant enzyme is not stimulated by calcium or calmodulin but still responds to guanyl nucleotides, fluoride and monoamines, suggesting a defect in the catalytic subunit itself (fly).

methods: classical (Pavlovian) odour–shock conditioning with a T-maze test
finding: A classical-conditioning version of the odour–shock paradigm gave strong learning (typically 95% of trained flies avoided the shock-paired odour), best when odour and shock overlapped and absent when the shock came first; memory decayed over 7 hours but was still present at 24, and amnesiac, rutabaga and dunce mutants learned appreciably but forgot rapidly within the first 30 minutes (fly).

In two mutants whose mushroom body input and output connections are largely interrupted, olfactory conditioning is abolished with electric shock and partly suppressed with sucrose reward, while the perception of the stimuli, spontaneous olfactory behaviour, colour discrimination learning and visual operant learning seem unaffected (fly).

methods: targeted expression of a constitutively active Gαs subunit
finding: Expressing a constitutively activated Gαs in the mushroom bodies, but not the central complex, abolished odour–shock learning while sensorimotor responses and gross mushroom body anatomy stayed normal, so olfactory learning depends on regulated Gs signalling in the mushroom bodies (fly).

Consolidated odour memory one day after extended training has two genetically distinct, independent components: anaesthesia-resistant memory, which decays within 4 days, resists cold, does not need protein synthesis and is disrupted by the radish mutation, and long-term memory, which shows no decay over 7 days, needs protein synthesis and does not need radish (fly).

Inducing a dominant-negative fly CREB transgene specifically and completely blocked long-term memory after odour conditioning while leaving learning and anaesthesia-resistant memory intact, suggesting that long-term memory needs new gene expression, probably through CREB family genes (fly).

Mutants with abnormal expression of the D1 dopamine receptor dDA1, which is enriched in the mushroom body, showed negligible shock-reinforced and moderately impaired sugar-reinforced odour learning with normal odour, shock and sugar responses, and restoring dDA1 in a subset of mushroom body neurons fully rescued both (fly).

methods: imaging of calcium and cAMP reporters
finding: Imaging cAMP in mushroom body neurons showed that depolarization followed by dopamine raises cAMP synergistically in the lobes, only with forward pairing at intervals like those needed for conditioning and depending on the rutabaga adenylyl cyclase, while octopamine was subadditive and raised cAMP elsewhere; raising cAMP facilitated calcium transients, and the authors propose rutabaga as a coincidence detector (fly).

methods: optogenetic pairing of odour and dopamine neuron activation
finding: Odour associations can be written and reversed trial by trial depending on the timing of the odour relative to dopaminergic reinforcement; reversals in learned odour attraction track bidirectional plasticity in the mushroom body, and two dopamine receptors, DopR1 and DopR2, coupled to different second messengers, direct synaptic depression or potentiation (fly).

methods: optogenetic activation of single dopamine neuron types paired with odour
finding: Memories formed by optogenetically activating individual dopamine neuron types differed widely in the training they needed, how fast they decayed, their capacity and how flexibly they were updated, and a single type could write or reduce an aversive memory, or write an appetitive one, depending on when it was activated relative to the odour (fly).

Dopamine inputs to the mushroom body modulate synaptic transmission with compartmental precision, letting individual neurons convey odour signals differently to each of their postsynaptic targets, and the dopamine neurons act as an interconnected network encoding external context and internal state, so the same odour is routed to different behavioural circuits (fly).

methods: optogenetic control of dopamine neuron subsets in behaving flies
finding: Optically controlling subsets of dopamine neurons in behaving flies mapped the aversive reinforcement signal to the 12 cells of the PPL1 cluster, which target restricted domains of the mushroom body vertical lobes and heel; activating them sufficed to write odour memories (fly).

methods: stimulation and block of identified neurons
finding: Stimulating neurons that express neuropeptide F (dNPF, an orthologue of mammalian NPY) mimicked hunger and promoted appetitive memory performance in fed flies; this needed the dNPF receptor in six dopamine neurons of one mushroom body region, whose block released memory performance in fed flies and whose stimulation suppressed it in hungry flies (fly).

methods: blocking and optogenetic activation of output neurons
finding: Glutamatergic M4/6 output neurons, whose dendrites overlap dopamine neuron projections at the tips of the β, β′ and γ lobes, are needed to express appetitive and aversive memory; conditioning changes their odour drive in either direction, blocking them in naive flies turns odour avoidance into approach, and activating them induces avoidance (fly).

methods: imaging after spaced and massed training
finding: Long-term odour memory needs protein synthesis in two MB-V3 output neurons of the vertical lobe: blocking it there, or knocking down the RNA-binding protein ORB in them, impairs long-term memory, their activity rises after spaced but not massed training, and their output is needed to retrieve the memory (fly).

In vivo recordings showed that Kenyon cell odour responses are highly selective and sparse compared with those of their projection-neuron inputs, owing to fast-decaying synaptic potentials, low convergence (about 10 projection neurons per Kenyon cell) and high firing thresholds, and that odour representations become less correlated from receptor neurons to Kenyon cells (fly).

methods: two-photon calcium imaging of over 100 Kenyon cells
finding: Imaging over 100 Kenyon cells at once showed sparse, distinct activity patterns for different odours, equally sparse for single odours, blends and natural smells and largely invariant across concentrations, with no spatial organization by tuning in the cell body layer (fly).

methods: knockdown of GABA synthesis in one neuron
finding: The single GABAergic APL neuron in each hemisphere innervates the mushroom bodies broadly; reducing its GABA synthesis enhanced olfactory learning, it responded to odour and shock, and odour–shock pairing left a memory trace in it, a reduced response to the trained odour (fly).

The amnesiac gene product, an apparent neuropeptide precursor, is not enriched in the mushroom bodies but strongly expressed in two large neurons that project over all their lobes; blocking vesicle recycling in these cells shortens memory as in amnesiac mutants, and restoring amn in them rescues olfactory memory (fly).

methods: cell-specific inhibition of synthesis and release
finding: Anaesthesia-resistant memory rises and falls with serotonin levels and needs serotonin released from the two DPM neurons onto the mushroom bodies, acting through d5HT1A receptors in α/β Kenyon cells, besides the Amnesiac peptide the same neurons release for anaesthesia-sensitive memory (fly).

The four mushroom body neuroblasts give rise only to mushroom body neurons and glia, each clone contributes to the whole structure with overlapping cell types, and each neuroblast can generate all the known mushroom body substructures on its own (fly).

A single mushroom body neuroblast generates three types of neurons in sequence: γ neurons before the mid-third larval instar, α′/β′ neurons until puparium formation, and α/β neurons after it; at metamorphosis the early-born γ neurons prune their larval axon branches and then project, unbranched, into the adult γ lobe (fly).

Clonal analysis of antennal lobe projection neurons showed that they are prespecified by lineage and birth order to send their dendrites to particular glomeruli, and so to connect with specific olfactory receptor neurons (fly).

A consortium of neurobiologists set out a hierarchical nomenclature of insect brain regions and fibre bundles, with the Drosophila brain as the reference, to standardize names and neuropil boundaries, including for connectomics (fly).

methods: expression of normal and mutant human α-synuclein
finding: Expressing normal or mutant human α-synuclein in flies produced adult-onset loss of dopaminergic neurons, filamentous inclusions containing α-synuclein and locomotor dysfunction, reproducing essential features of Parkinson’s disease (fly).

Flies lacking parkin, a ubiquitin–protein ligase whose loss causes a familial juvenile parkinsonism, have reduced lifespan, locomotor defects from apoptotic death of muscle subsets and male sterility, with mitochondrial pathology as the earliest sign (fly).

methods: expression of human Aβ40 or Aβ42 in the brain
finding: Expressing human Aβ42 in the fly brain caused diffuse amyloid deposits, age-dependent learning defects and extensive neurodegeneration, whereas Aβ40 caused only age-dependent learning defects (fly).

Flies lacking dfmr1 activity, a model of fragile X syndrome, have courtship, courtship-memory and mushroom body defects that treatment with metabotropic glutamate receptor antagonists or lithium rescues, implicating enhanced mGluR signalling (fly).

methods: targeted expression of an expanded-polyglutamine SCA3 fragment
finding: Expressing a fragment of the spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 protein with an expanded polyglutamine repeat caused nuclear inclusions and late-onset degeneration, to which neurons were especially susceptible; inclusions alone did not suffice for degeneration, and the anti-apoptotic gene P35 mitigated it (fly).

A screen of 9,000 mutant lines found minisleep, which sleeps a third of the normal amount with preserved sleep homeostasis and no impairment from sleep deprivation, and carries a point mutation in the Shaker potassium channel; other Shaker alleles also sleep little, and short-sleeping Shaker flies live shorter lives (fly).

Locus coeruleus tyrosine-hydroxylase neurons project more profusely to the hippocampus than VTA ones, and environmental novelty drives their firing; optogenetically activating them mimicked the novelty-induced enhancement of everyday memory and produced long-lasting potentiation of CA1 transmission. Both effects were blocked by hippocampal D1/D5 (not adrenergic) antagonists, consistent with co-release of dopamine from LC terminals (mouse).

Dopaminergic axons and dopamine release in the dorsal hippocampus arise from the locus coeruleus rather than the VTA, which has few axons there; photostimulating LC axons raised dorsal-hippocampal dopamine and enhanced spatial object recognition and attention through D1/D5 receptors (mouse).

Optogenetic activation of serotonergic terminals in hippocampal CA1 potentiated CA3-to-CA1 transmission through 5-HT4 receptors and enhanced spatial memory, while silencing them impaired it; systemic 5-HT4 modulation bidirectionally changed memory formation (mouse).

Selective stimulation of serotonergic median raphe neurons rapidly and synaptically activated hippocampal interneurons, producing disynaptic GABAergic inhibition across the circuit; this fast, glutamate/5-HT co-transmission is a direct synaptic (not only metabotropic) form of subcortical control of hippocampal processing (rat).

Optogenetic activation of medial septal cholinergic neurons abolished hippocampal sharp-wave ripples, suppressed slow and supratheta bands and robustly increased theta power and coherence, showing that septal acetylcholine can both enhance theta and suppress peri-theta rhythms (mouse).

Septal cholinergic input timed relative to Schaffer-collateral stimulation induced different forms of CA1 plasticity: alpha7-nicotinic LTP when acetylcholine arrived ~100 ms before, short-term depression at ~10 ms before, and muscarinic LTP when it followed by ~10 ms; amyloid-beta disrupted these forms (rat).

Photostimulation of locus coeruleus noradrenergic fibers in the basolateral amygdala evoked local norepinephrine release, altered BLA activity, conditioned aversion and increased anxiety-like behavior; the anxiety phenotype was mediated by beta-adrenergic receptors in the BLA (mouse).

VTA dopamine axons innervating the basal amygdala responded to both rewards and punishments and acquired responses to cues predicting them; responses to food-predicting cues were attenuated by satiety while those to punishment persisted, providing a motivational-salience signal to intermingled appetitive and aversive basal-amygdala neurons (mouse).

Optogenetic release of acetylcholine from basal forebrain cholinergic axons in the basolateral amygdala evoked fast nicotinic EPSPs in late-firing interneurons and, in principal neurons, state-dependent muscarinic (M1) IPSPs at low firing but prolonged afterdepolarizations at higher firing, enhancing signal-to-noise and potentially aiding fear-conditioning associations (mouse).

Basal forebrain and brainstem cholinergic neurons differentially drove the amygdala: basal forebrain input to the basal nucleus released acetylcholine, produced biphasic inhibition-excitation and strengthened theta and gamma rhythms, while brainstem input excited the central lateral division via glutamate; driving them produced opposing appetitive and defensive learning-related behaviors (mouse).

Stimulating cholinergic terminals in the basolateral amygdala during fear conditioning slowed extinction while inhibiting them reduced acquisition; endogenous acetylcholine enhanced principal-neuron firing and glutamatergic transmission and induced LTP of cortical-amygdala circuits (mouse).

Dorsal raphe serotonin neurons form parallel sub-systems with complementary projections: amygdala-projecting serotonin neurons and frontal-cortex-projecting ones differ in inputs, collateralization and responses to aversive stimuli, and gain- and loss-of-function showed the amygdala-projecting population promotes anxiety-like behavior (mouse).

Horseradish-peroxidase tracing showed a bilateral locus coeruleus projection to cat primary visual cortex, and electrically stimulating the LC suppressed activity in most layer II-IV cells (beta-adrenergic) and facilitated many layer V-VI cells (alpha- and beta-adrenergic), so LC noradrenaline controls each cortical layer differently (cat).

Quantifying dopamine-beta-hydroxylase (release) and norepinephrine-transporter (reuptake) axon segments across macaque V1 and V2 confirmed locus coeruleus noradrenergic innervation of primary visual cortex, denser in V2 than V1, with release and reuptake sites differently distributed across layers (macaque).

Optogenetic activation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons or their V1 axon terminals improved visual-discrimination performance trial by trial, enhanced visual responses and desynchronized spiking in V1, while inactivation impaired performance and visual responses (mouse).

Optogenetic stimulation of the dorsal raphe nucleus had separable suppressive effects on visual cortex: 5-HT1A receptors divisively suppressed spontaneous activity while 5-HT2A receptors divisively scaled visual-response gain, accounting for contrast normalization of population responses (mouse).

Photostimulating VTA dopamine neurons or their insular-cortex terminals improved the salience that consolidates a subthreshold taste memory without changing palatability, and blocking D1-like receptors in the insula impaired consolidation of innate and conditioned aversive taste memories (mouse).

Activity in the VTA-to-insular-cortex dopaminergic pathway was necessary for object-recognition memory: photostimulation during short training enabled acquisition while photoinhibition during long training prevented it, and blocking insular D1-like receptors abolished the enhancement, without changing exploration (mouse).

The rostral agranular insular cortex of the rat has a dense dopamine innervation arising mainly from the ipsilateral VTA/substantia nigra, from neurons distinct from those projecting to medial prefrontal cortex, with dopamine fibers apposing GABAergic interneurons that gate limbic-projecting output (rat).

Reversibly inactivating the nucleus basalis magnocellularis cut acetylcholine release in the insular cortex and impaired acquisition, but not retrieval, of conditioned taste aversion, implicating basal-forebrain cholinergic input to the insula in early taste-memory formation (rat).

Histaminergic manipulation of the nucleus basalis magnocellularis and insular cortex reduced cortical acetylcholine release and impaired conditioned-taste-aversion memory, showing that basal-forebrain cholinergic input to the insula is tuned by histamine during taste-memory formation (rat).

Systematic input-output mapping of VTA dopamine neurons showed that those projecting to lateral and medial nucleus accumbens innervate largely non-overlapping targets and receive biased inputs, defining parallel mesostriatal dopamine channels including a cortex-to-lateral-accumbens reinforcing circuit (mouse).

Pedunculopontine cholinergic neurons drive dissociable midbrain pathways: their terminals in the ventral substantia nigra pars compacta control locomotion while those in the VTA control reinforcement, and laterodorsal tegmental cholinergic terminals in the VTA also produce reinforcement (rat).

methods: in vivo juxtacellular recording and labeling
finding: Pedunculopontine and laterodorsal tegmental cholinergic axons innervate segregated VTA dopamine populations: laterodorsal input enhanced bursting of mesolimbic dopamine neurons excited by aversive stimuli, while pedunculopontine input drove a distinct population inhibited by them, with opposite roles in locomotion (rat).

Bidirectional optogenetic modulation of serotonin release from dorsal raphe neurons in the nucleus accumbens bidirectionally changed sociability, and activating these 5-HT neurons rescued social deficits in a 16p11.2 autism-model mouse through accumbal 5-HT1b receptors (mouse).

Octopus gonadotropin-releasing hormone (oct-GnRH) mRNA and peptide were found in cell bodies of 10 of 19 brain lobes, with fibers throughout the neuropils and in peripheral organs; the authors place oct-GnRH in a subpedunculate/olfactory-lobe-optic-gland-gonad axis analogous to the vertebrate hypothalamo-hypophysial-gonadal axis and acting on higher functions (Octopus vulgaris).

Reviewing the nervous control of octopus reproduction: the subpedunculate lobe (via FMRFamide) inhibits and the olfactory lobe (rich in gonadotropin-releasing hormone and other neuropeptides) is thought to excite optic-gland gonadotropin release, making the olfactory lobe an integrative centre linking distant chemical stimuli to sexual maturation (Octopus vulgaris).

FMRFamide-like and GnRH-like immunoreactivity in the octopus brain and optic gland: the subpedunculate area appears to source the FMRFamide-like peptide and the posterior olfactory lobule the GnRH-like peptide, both sending fibers through the optic-gland nerve onto glandular cells, consistent with neuropeptidergic control of the optic gland (Octopus vulgaris).

At least 40% of all locus coeruleus neurons project to the olfactory bulb, a projection roughly ten times denser than to any other part of the cerebral cortex, identifying an unexpectedly rich noradrenergic LC-to-olfactory-bulb pathway (rat).

Activating the locus coeruleus, the sole noradrenergic source of the main olfactory bulb, increased the excitatory responses of mitral cells to weak (perithreshold) olfactory-nerve input by about 67% without changing baseline firing, suggesting LC noradrenaline enhances detection of weak odors (rat).

Locus coeruleus noradrenergic neurons project directly to the olfactory bulb and anterior piriform cortex; noradrenaline bidirectionally modulated bulb mitral cells via inhibitory inputs and reduced piriform pyramidal excitability via alpha2 receptors, and activating the projection accelerated odor discrimination while inactivation impaired detection and discrimination (mouse).

Serotonergic fibers from the dorsal raphe modulate sensory input to olfactory-bulb glomeruli: 5-HT2C activation amplified odor-evoked activity in a subset of juxtaglomerular cells while attenuating glutamate release from olfactory-receptor-neuron terminals via GABA-B, and electrically stimulating the dorsal raphe attenuated odor-evoked responses (mouse).

Brief optogenetic activation of raphe axons in the olfactory bulb, through dual release of serotonin and glutamate, excited tufted cells and potentiated their odor responses while bidirectionally modulating mitral cells to improve odor pattern separation, a fast sub-second top-down modulation of parallel output channels (mouse).

Optogenetic activation of basal forebrain cholinergic axons in the olfactory bulb rapidly and transiently increased mitral/tufted-cell spiking, adding an excitatory bias to odor coding independent of the strength or polarity of the odorant response and dependent on local cholinergic signaling (mouse).

Optogenetic activation of basal-forebrain (horizontal diagonal band) cholinergic neurons inhibited spontaneous firing of all major olfactory-bulb cell types yet sharpened mitral/tufted-cell odor tuning and potentiated periglomerular and granule-cell responses, supporting a role in olfactory discrimination (mouse).

Octopamine-immunoreactive ventral unpaired median neurons of the subesophageal ganglion send ascending neurites that supply the antennal-lobe glomeruli, the mushroom-body calyces, the lateral protocerebrum, the central complex (protocerebral bridge, fan-shaped body and ellipsoid body) and the lobula complex, mapping a brain-wide octopaminergic system in the fruit fly (Drosophila).

Single-cell labeling resolved 27 types of octopaminergic neuron in the adult Drosophila brain; most separate their dendrites, confined to specific regions, from presynaptic terminals that each target different defined neuropils across the brain, so octopaminergic cells could act as combinatorial modules modulating distinct processes (Drosophila).

Mouse medial septal cholinergic neurons co-transmit acetylcholine and GABA from distinct vesicle populations to hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells and interneurons; the fast GABAergic component suppresses sharp-wave ripples in hippocampal slices.

Identifies Ch1–Ch4 cholinergic mapping in the rhesus monkey: Ch1 (medial septum) and Ch2/Ch3 (diagonal band) innervate hippocampus and entorhinal cortex, while Ch4 (nucleus basalis/substantia innominata) provides topographically organized projections to frontoparietal, cingulate, temporal, and sensory cortices and the amygdala.
